increasing MBBS & PG seats in Government Medical Colleges with a cost ceiling of ₹1.20 crore 
per seat with similar funding pattern between Central and State/UT Governments. Under these 
schemes, 4977 MBBS seats and 8058 PG seats have been approved across the country so far.  
 
1.10 Monitoring, Fraud Control and Grievance Redressal 
Recommendation 
1.10.1 The Committee would like to place an emphasis in applying behavioural science insights 
to increase the uptake of the PMJAY Scheme. Keeping in view some of the recent behavioural 
studies, the Committee suggests that PMJAY messaging to the targeted population can be revised 
by including the following behavioural insights: 
 Simplification: PMJAY messaging to contain short and simplified text with clear 
behavioural instruction to register with the Scheme. 
 Social norms: People simulate behaviour when they see that others are also doing it. 
PMJAY messaging can be designed in such a way that carries a strong message that 
others are doing it. Moreover, behavioural studies indicate that people are risk-seeking 
over losses but risk-averse over gains. Gain-framed PMJAY messaging will prove to be 
effective. 
(Para 3.2.3(i) (d) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.10.2 As on 01.05.2024, over 6.96 crore hospital admission worth over ₹ 94,225 crore have 
been authorized under the scheme out of which 1.98 crore hospital admission have been 

16 
 
authorized under the scheme during 2023-24. This clearly manifests that the scheme uptake has 
significantly increased over years with the increasing beneficiary awareness.   
1.10.3 In this regard, it is pertinent to note that NHA has a comprehensive media and outreach 
strategy to spread awareness and empowering the beneficiaries about their entitlements and rights 
under the scheme has been followed. This includes the use of media vehicles such as outdoor 
media, digital display at ticket counters across various railway stations, announcements at major 
bus stations, passenger train branding, national and regional press coverage, op-eds and 
advertorials in print media, radio campaign, telecast of beneficiary testimonials via Doordarshan, 
mass messaging, etc. Further, NHA is working on nudge messaging also for the eligible 
beneficiaries under the scheme. 
1.10.4 Along with this, NHA publishes success stories along with beneficiary testimonials who 
have availed benefits under the scheme on social media platforms and through other media 
vehicles.  
1.10.5  Messages are sent to beneficiaries at different stages of card creation and service delivery. 
The inputs of the Committee have been noted regarding behavioural change for necessary action.  
 
1.11 Importance to Medical Ethics 
Recommendation 
1.11.1 The Committee is of the opinion that maintaining medical ethics and avoiding 
unnecessary procedures, tests, and over-prescription is a concern, as it can lead to rising costs 
and potential harm to patients. The Government should give impetus to value education and 
ethics in medical curriculum and training workshops to sensitise the staff involved in the 
implementation of the scheme that maintaining small ethical standards would bring significant 
results. 
(Para 3.2.3(iii) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.11.2 For the treatments under PM-JAY, NHA has developed a total of 28 sets of 675 Standard 
Treatment Guidelines (STGs) in order to ensure appropriate healthcare delivery for specific 
clinical circumstances. STGs have been integrated in TMS for assisting adjudicators in 
processing of request for pre-authorizations and claims. 
1.11.3 Further, National Health Authority has setup a National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) with the 
primary responsibility of prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under PM-JAY. 
Further, all States/UTs have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State level to 
instrumentalize anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level. 

17 
 
1.11.4 With respect to the upgrades in the system, it may kindly be noted that NHA has been 
using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to detect suspicious 
transactions / potential frauds in AB PM-JAY. Technologies deployed include rule-based triggers 
and Machine Learning algorithms, fuzzy logic, image classification and de-duplication, etc. 
1.11.5 The Government has taken significant steps to incorporate value education into medical 
curriculum and training programs. Section 25 (1)(b) of NMC Act, 2019 provides that Post-
Graduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB) under NMC develop competency based dynamic 
curriculum at postgraduate level and super-speciality level in accordance with the regulations 
made under this Act, with a view to develop appropriate skill, knowledge, attitude, values and 
ethics among postgraduates and super-specialists to provide healthcare, impart medical education 
and conduct medical research. 
1.11.6 In response to above quoted section, NMC Post Graduate Medical Education Regulations, 
2023 or “PGMER-23” in its abbreviated form, provides that all postgraduate students shall 
complete course in ethics including Good Clinical Practices and Good Laboratory Practices, 
whichever is relevant to them, to be conducted by Institutions/Universities. The students are 
expected to complete the course in the first year. No post-graduate student shall be permitted to 
appear in the examination without the above certification. Further, it shall be the duty of all 
concerned universities with the medical institutions under them, to partner with the NMC to 
provide training in clinical and practical skills along with theoretical knowledge, laying emphasis 
upon attitude, ethics and communication skills to ensure imparting competency-based medical 
education. 
 
1.12 Technology and Data Security 
Recommendation  
 
1.12.1 The Committee has been informed that the personal details and medical history of the 
beneficiaries under PMJAY are maintained by the NHA through various modules of their IT 
platform. The beneficiaries may visit multiple doctors. The digital record would help the doctor 
to see the medical history of the beneficiary with his/her consent. The NHA has also maintained a 
standardised registry containing the list of all the hospitals, which is called the Healthcare 
Facility Registry, a list of all the healthcare professionals, doctors, nurses, a list of all labs, a list 
of all the drugs, etc. These initiatives are significant to make the PMJAY scheme cashless, 
paperless, portable, transparent, etc. However, the Committee would also like to highlight that 
safeguarding patient data and ensuring the security of health information systems are vital to 
prevent data breaches and misuse. The Government must ensure robust IT infrastructure with 
quality encryption and safeguards. 
(Para 3.2.3 (iv) (a) of the Report) 

18 
 
Action Taken 
1.12.2 The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) aims to develop the backbone necessary 
to support the integrated digital health infrastructure of the country. It will bridge the existing gap 
amongst different stakeholders of healthcare ecosystem through digital highways. The Mission 
aims to create an integrated healthcare system that will link practitioners and patients digitally by 
giving them access to real-time health records. 
1.12.3 Under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission different registries are being created. Under 
ABDM, Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) is being created for every citizen, which 
shall work like her digital health-records wallet. Similarly, Healthcare Professionals Registry 
(HPR), a comprehensive repository of all healthcare professionals involved in delivery of 
healthcare services across both modern and traditional systems of medicine is being created. 
Further, Health Facility Registry (HFR) is a comprehensive repository of health facilities of the 
nation across different systems of medicine. It includes both public and private health facilities 
including hospitals, clinics, diagnostic laboratories and imaging centres, pharmacies, etc. As on 
16/05/2024, 61.46 crore ABHA cards have been created and 38.10 crore health records have been 
linked. Further, 2.67 lakh health facilities have been verified on HFR and 3.49 lakh healthcare 
professionals have been verified on HPR. 
1.12.4 Under AB PM-JAY, ABHA ID of the beneficiary has been integrated with PM-JAY ID to 
ensure seamless integration with larger healthcare ecosystem. 
1.12.5 National Health Authority (NHA) is committed to the protection of beneficiaries’ privacy 
and is taking the necessary steps to protect the personal data belonging to beneficiaries’ or any 
individual who is a part of Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY). 
1.12.6 The repository in which NHA stores data is RDBMS (Relational Database management 
System) which has been setup in the NHA data center. PII (Personal Identifiable Information) of 
the beneficiary is stored in RDBMS in encrypted format.  
1.12.7 NHA has also engaged Telecom Consultants of India Limited (TCIL) as Security 
Operation Center (SOC) which monitors security postures (alerts & incidents) of the cloud 
infrastructure. They also conduct Security Assessment of all NHA Apps. They use the Threat 
Intelligence tools to ensure all known threats are configured in the rules and IOCs informed by 
various security agencies are blocked immediately to secure NHA Infrastructure. NHA also has a 
team of security experts over and above the security experts of Master Service Provider & Cloud 
Service Provider, who tracks the performance of IT system. 
1.13       Technology and Data Security 
Recommendation  
 

19 
 
1.13.1 The Committee also believes that the Government should give impetus to trust-building 
campaigns as some of the beneficiaries may hesitate to join the scheme of misleading information 
regarding breaches of their personal and medical data security. The Committee has also been 
informed that some of the healthcare professionals have also raised data security concerns and 
are hesitating to register at the NHA registry. The Government must address these concerns 
through continuous interaction and trust-building initiatives. 
(Para 3.2.3 (iv) (b) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.13.2 Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is designed on the principle of privacy 
preserving federated data architecture that is essential for enhancing the  security  and  privacy  of  
the  personal  and  sensitive  information  of  the citizens while ensuring interoperability and 
technological flexibility and independence. Therefore, data is not centralized but rather stored 
within the hospitals/facilities where it originates. Health data is always created and stored by 
healthcare providers. ABDM only facilitates secure data exchange between the intended 
stakeholders on ABDM network after the patient’s consent. Consequently, the responsibility for 
implementing robust data security mechanisms also falls upon these hospitals/facilities, where the 
data is stored. 
1.13.3 Only the data collected for registries such as the ABHA registry, Healthcare Professional 
Registry, and Healthcare Facility Registry is stored centrally. This central storage is imperative as 
these datasets play a crucial role in ensuring interoperability, trust, identification, and establishing 
a single source of truth across various digital health systems. 
1.13.4 Data sharing is allowed based in compliance with the ABDM Health Data Management 
Policy (“HDM Policy”) which has the principle of “Security and Privacy by Design” for the 
protection of individuals’ personal digital health privacy at its core. It acts as a guidance 
document across the National Digital Health Ecosystem (NDHE) and sets out the minimum 
standards for data privacy protection that should be followed to ensure compliance with relevant 
and applicable law, rules and regulations. 
1.13.5 The importance of trust-building campaigns, especially considering potential 
misinformation surrounding data security breaches is acknowledged. Extensive IEC in the form 
of radio spots, print media and IRCTC website have been initiated and will be continued to 
address these concerns and communicating the privacy related safeguards in ABDM so that 
beneficiaries feel confident in participating in the ABDM. 
1.13.6 In the National Healthcare Provider Registry (NHPR), healthcare professionals grant 
consent for the visibility of their profiles (public display) during registration. Additionally, 
professionals have the option to choose which fields they wish to display publicly. Consequently, 
based on their consent, specific fields within their profile, such as mobile numbers or email 
addresses, may be visible or not visible in the public domain as per their preference. We 
understand that some healthcare professionals may also have reservations regarding data security, 

20 
 
and we are actively working to engage with them directly and/or through their professional 
associations to address their concerns.  
 
1.14 Indirect Cost and Expenditure Beyond the cover of ₹ 5 lakh 
Recommendation  
 
1.14.1 The Committee has seen that, while interacting with the beneficiaries of Ayushman 
Bharat, even if the beneficiaries are insured, they must bear the high indirect cost that might go 
beyond their ability to pay. To address the catastrophic financial burden on poor patients and to 
achieve the objective of PMJAY, the Government needs to cover this indirect financial loss for a 
poor patient for whom this cost is not negligible. 
(Para 3.2.3(v) (a) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.14.2 AB PM-JAY provides health cover of up to ₹ 5 lakh per family per year for secondary 
and tertiary care hospitalization. The treatment packages under AB PM-JAY are very 
comprehensive which includes pre-hospitalization expenses including diagnostics, 
premedication, pre-anaesthetic examination, and consultation relevant to the present disease for 
up to 3 days and the package amount also covers post-hospitalization expenses including drug 
expenses for up to 15-days under this scheme. 
1.14.3 However, few States and UTs provide additional benefits in terms of transport allowance 
etc. to the scheme beneficiaries with the intent to reduce OOPE. 
1.14.4 The suggestions of the Committee regarding covering indirect expenses are noted.  
 
1.15 Indirect Cost and Expenditure Beyond the Cover of ₹ 5 lakhs 
 
Recommendation  
 
1.15.1 The Committee, while interacting with both private and government hospitals, has noted 
that some of the complex and high-end surgeries or chronic treatment cost more than the sum of 
₹ 5 lakhs covered under the PMJAY. Also, some of the costly procedures and surgeries are not 
covered under the scheme. To address such issues, some of the hospitals have set an example by 
successfully attracting Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds and private investment to 
create funds to bear the expenditure of beneficiaries for the cost of treatment over and above the 
insured sum of ₹ 5 lakhs. The Government need to implement such practices across the country 
to make PM-JAY more and more effective and beneficial for the poor sections of the society. 
Further, in many cases, the amount of ₹ 5 lakhs may not be utilised by every patient/family. Only 
in cases of serious diseases and other surgeries, this amount is utilised. Apart from Rashtriya 

21 
 
Arogya Nidhi, the Government should consider the creation of some special purpose vehicle or 
arrangement to cater to fill the gap in such special cases in a more structured manner. 
(Para 3.2.3 (v) (b) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.15.2 With regard to the limit of ₹ 5 lakhs, it may be noted that 99.4% of expenditure incurred 
per treatment cycle is usually below ₹ 2 lakhs. Therefore, almost all treatments are covered under 
AB PM-JAY and the existing wallet of ₹ 5 lakhs is sufficient for providing treatment to the 
beneficiaries. Currently, PMJAY covers 1949 procedures across 27 specialities. High-end 
treatments like bone marrow transplant, renal transplant, medical and radiation oncology are 
covered under AB PM-JAY. 
1.15.3 Further, under Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN), eligible beneficiaries are provided higher 
cover for identified treatment. 
1.15.4 Further, few States have decided to expand the benefit cover under the scheme. Further, 
few SHAs have created a corpus using certain percentage of the claim revenues earned under by 
Government hospitals under the scheme to provide additional support for high end treatment 
beyond 5 lakhs. 
1.15.5 In view of the above, treatment requirement of the beneficiaries is mostly met. However, 
suggestion of the Committee is noted.  
 
1.16 Need to expand the treatment procedures covered under PM-JAY 
Recommendation  
 
1.16.1 The Committee has come to know that some costly procedures and serious diseases are 
not included in the PMJAY. Further, the OPD expenses are not covered by the scheme and are 
considered only in the case of inpatients. The Committee recommends that the coverage of 
procedures and surgeries under PM-JAY needs to be increased. Further, the Committee suggests 
that the rates under the health benefit packages (HBP) of PM-JAY must be revised frequently and 
kept updated vis-à-vis the present market rates 
 
 (Para 3.2.3(vi) of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.16.2 Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY was launched as part of Ayushman Bharat, making a shift 
from a sectoral and segmented approach of health service delivery to comprehensive need-based 

22 
 
healthcare service. This involved two interrelated components viz. PM-JAY for secondary and 
tertiary care and Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) to cater to primary 
healthcare needs of the scheme.  
1.16.3 Further, it may kindly be noted that the treatment packages under AB PM-JAY are very 
comprehensive and consists of 1949 procedures across 27 specialties which also includes 1 
unspecified package to include such packages not specified in the Health Benefit Package. 
Further, treatment covered under AB PM-JAY includes medical & radiation oncology, renal 
transplant, bone-marrow transplant etc. 
1.16.4 With respect to the rates and packages defined under PM-JAY, it is important to note that 
the Health Benefit packages used under AB PM-JAY have been revised and rationalized over the 
years. To begin with, AB PM-JAY initially had 1393 treatment packages. However, the fifth and 
the latest Health Benefit package - HBP 2022 was launched in April 2022 wherein a total of 365 
procedures have been added and rates have been revised upwards in case of 832 procedures. HBP 
2022 consists of 1949 procedures including 1 unspecified package across 27 specialities. Further, 
NHA is again undertaking the review exercise for the HBP and shall be taken up as per the 
recommendation/suggestion received in this regard. 
 
1.17 Inclusion of Above Poverty Line (APL) middle-class people in the PMJAY 
Recommendation  
 
1.17.1 The Committee is of the view that there are many lower middle-class people who fall in 
the APL category, and they are just above the BPL and the inclusion criteria for the PMJAY. 
Such people are in dire need of this scheme. The report of NITI Aayog titled “Health Insurance 
for India’s Missing Middle” also suggests that even after the implementation of the PMJAY, at 
least 30% of the population (over 40 crore individuals) still lack any form of financial protection 
for health. Adverse health events can lead to financial hardship and even push them into poverty. 
They are characterized by informal employment with unstable incomes and a lack of social 
security benefits. The Committee believes that the Government should consider expanding the 
base of beneficiaries to be covered under the PMJAY by including more categories in eligibility 
criteria. This is also in line with the eventual objective of the Government to attain the SDG goal 
of the UHC. 
 (Para 3.2.3(vii) of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.17.2 A total of 12 crore beneficiary families have been covered under PMJAY. Government of 
India has decided to include 37.18 lakh ASHAs/AWWs/AWHs included under the scheme. In 

23 
 
addition, many States have expanded the coverage under the scheme and 13 States/UTs are 
implementing near Universal Health Coverage. 
1.17.3 Further, NHA is working in collaboration with different Ministries to expand the 
coverage under AB PM-JAY ecosystem to eligible population through convergence of existing 
healthcare cover. Recently, NHA entered an MoU with the Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment (MoSJE) to expand healthcare services to manual scavengers, transgenders, etc. 
1.17.4 NHA is also engaging with NITI Aayog and different Ministries to identify potential 
missing groups and devise mechanisms to extend healthcare protection to them by using different 
modes of financing.  
 
1.18 Guidelines and Mechanism to Govern Employment and Conduct of Arogya Mitras 
Recommendation  
 
1.18.1 The Committee has been informed that the Central Government has not issued any 
standard guidelines to employ Arogya Mitras under the PMJAY. There are different 
arrangements to employ them and to pay them any honorarium across the States. In some States, 
they are retired or serving employees of the same hospital for which additional payment is made 
to them for their services. They help the patients in their registration and provide guidance 
during the treatment. The Committee recommends that the Central Government should issue 
guidelines and minimum qualifications to be complied with by the States while employing Arogya 
Mitras. The Government should devise a mechanism to monitor the conduct and ethical 
behaviour of Arogya Mitras. 
 (Para 3.2.3(viii) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.18.2 NHA has issued guidelines for onboarding of PMAMs where suggestive criteria for 
selection of PMAMs have been defined which are as follows: 
● Completed 10+2 from a recognized institution (Preferably Graduates) 
● Basic proficiency in computer operations 
● Completed the Pradhan Mantri Arogya Mitra Training Course and passed the respective 
course exam/certification. 
● Possessing fluent communication skills in Hindi/ English and Local language of the State/ 
region 
● Having adequate functional computer literacy which shall include understanding of 
Microsoft Office Suite and navigating through Internet Portals. 
● Preference to be given to Female Candidates for the position of Pradhan Mantri Arogya 
Mitra. 

24 
 
● Existing staff of Government hospitals can also be nominated to act as Pradhan Mantri 
Arogya Mitra by the State Government. 
1.18.3 However, the responsibility with regard to engagement of PMAMs rests with the 
States/UTs. 
1.18.4 As regards grievances of any misconduct and any unethical behavior, beneficiaries can 
register online/offline complaint through national call centre (14555) or on grievance redressal 
portal (https://cgrms.PM-JAY.gov.in/) or through any other medium. All such grievances are 
immediately assigned to respective authorities at the States or national level. Also, it is pertinent 
to note that post discharge of beneficiaries, the feedback mechanism also captures input with 
regard to PMAMs. Further, the input received on the matter has been noted.

2.1 Healthcare and Health Insurance Schemes in Other Countries 
Recommendation 
2.1.1 The Committee notes that the experiences of Thailand, China, and Latin American 
countries demonstrate the difficulty of increasing health coverage in the informal/unorganized 
sector. Thailand made good progress in UHC by fully subsidizing the informal sector, while 
China has partially subsidized that segment. However, China’s experience also indicates the 
possibility of sustained coverage through a contributory and voluntary scheme. Further, the 
examples from Latin America highlight that adverse selection and inadequate risk-pooling is a 
pressing challenge for voluntary contributory schemes targeted towards the informal sector. The 
adverse selection due to opting out of high-income people reduces cross-subsidisation, leading to 
high premiums and inequality in access to healthcare.  
(Para 1.4.10 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.1.2 The suggestions from the Committee regarding different models for extending healthcare 
cover to different population groups have been noted.  
Recommendation 
2.1.3 The Committee is of the view that the Government may consider some of the provisions of 
the Affordable Care Act of United States for inclusion in Ayushman Bharat. By including some 
sections of the persons falling in APL category, the provisions for 'employer mandate' to provide 
health insurance to the employee and his family, subsuming of specific schemes for children and 
senior citizens, tax incentives and disincentives to corporate regarding healthcare are some of 
the measures worth including in the Ayushman Bharat Scheme and PMJAY. 
(Para 1.4.11 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.1.4 As of now, the benefit coverage under AB PM-JAY is completely funded by the Central 
and State Government together. 
2.1.5 Further, employees working in establishments with 10 or more persons (20 or more in 
some states) whose monthly wages do not exceed ₹ 21,000 are covered under ESIC. In such 
cases, collective contribution from employees is mandated which are used for extending different 
kinds of services including healthcare. NHA and ESIC are working towards establishing 

26 
 
synergies between PM-JAY and healthcare services provided under ESIC. As on date, ESIC 
beneficiaries can avail healthcare services under AB PM-JAY in 157 districts. 
2.2 Financing Mechanism 
Recommendation 
2.2.1 The Committee notes that the fund released by the Central Government during the last 
five years, from 2018-19 to 2022-23, towards PM-JAY is around ₹ 17,000 crore, of which ₹ 
6,180 crore were released in the last financial year. Also, except for the last financial year, the 
fund utilization was much less as compared to the budget estimation. The Government should 
take steps to ensure higher and more efficient utilization of funds allocated in the budget. The 
Committee would further like to state that the budget of ₹ 6,000-7,000 crore allocated as the 
share of the Central Government is much less for 33 States/UTs. The Committee suggests that the 
budget allocation for the scheme should be increased as the PM-JAY is the keystone scheme of 
the Government in achieving the UHC. For this purpose, other old/peripheral schemes of the 
Government in the healthcare sector may be subsumed or integrated with PM-JAY so that the 
unutilized funds, resources, and manpower involved in those schemes may be utilized for the 
efficient implementation of PMJAY. 
(Para 2.4.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.2.2 The budget allocated for the financial year 2018-19 was ₹ 2400 crore out of which 
₹1849.5 crore has been released to States/UTs. Further, the revised budgetary allocation for the 
financial year 2019-20 was ₹ 3,200 crore out of which ₹2992.9 crore have been released to 
States/UTs as part of central share of funds. During 2019-20, the budgetary allocation was 
increased to ₹ 6400 crore which was revised to ₹ 3,200 crore, of which ₹ 2,992.9 crore has been 
released to States and UTs. Further, ₹ 6400 crore were allocated for the financial year 2020-21 
and 2021-22 out of which ₹ 2544.1 crore and ₹ 2940.6 crore respectively have been released to 
States/UTs. This shortfall may be attributed to low utilization as the scheme was in its initial full 
year of implementation. Also, the uptake of scheme was affected during COVID. 
2.2.3 For the FY 2022-23, ₹ 6412 crore was allocated and the funds allocated have been fully 
utilized other than the North-East component. Further, the budget allocated for the financial year 
2023-24 is ₹ 7,200 crore (including ₹ 569 crore for capital expenditure and headquarter 
expenditure) out of which ₹ 6060.4 crore have been released to States / UTs implementing AB 
PM-JAY as part of the Central share of funds.  
2.2.4 Along with this, it is pertinent to note that as per Cabinet approval, the budget estimate for 
the upcoming Financial Years i.e. FY 2024-25 and 2025-26 has been revised to ₹ 8,498 crore for 
each FY anticipating the increase in scheme uptake.  
 

27 
 
2.3 Coverage of beneficiaries under PMJAY 
Recommendation 
2.3.1 The Committee came to know of the instances of delay in approval of empanelment of 
hospitals. In some cases, the delays beyond the stipulated period of 30 days ranged from 1 day to 
44 months. The Committee is of the view that the Government should review the procedures in 
this regard and take necessary steps to reduce the pendency in such approvals after carrying out 
all effective checks. 
(Para 2.5.11 of the Report)

2.3.2 The decision regarding the empanelment of the hospitals comes under the purview of 
respective State Government. However, NHA monitors this as part of performance indicators of 
the scheme and has issued guidelines to SHAs regularly regarding pending empanelment 
requests.  
2.3.3 The pendency is attributed to the delay in reply from the hospitals with the queries raised

2.3.4 Communication is sent to respective stakeholders via e-mail, SMS, webinars, various

2.3.5 Further, NHA is working with the stakeholders for process re-engineering to streamline

2.4 Best Practices in Providing UHC 
Recommendation 
2.4.1 The Ministry, in coordination with NHA and SHAs, should accelerate and intensify the 
IEC activities. The camps at village and block levels should be organised in a planned manner to 
increase awareness about the scheme and to fast-pace the registration of eligible beneficiaries. 
Civil societies, NGOs and local-level officials need to be involved in making these camps 
successful. The ration shops may also be roped in to increase awareness among the local masses, 
which could play a significant role in saturating beneficiary coverage across all the districts. 
Further, the verification of genuine beneficiaries is necessary to prevent the leakage of funds. 
The practice followed in Chandigarh should be implemented across the country, particularly in 
urban areas where the proportion of the migratory population is high, to ensure the genuineness 
of beneficiaries. A dedicated cell should be formed in every district for cross-checking of 
documents, telephonic verification, and door-to-door field verifications with a special focus on 
non-KYC beneficiaries. The success stories and testimonials of PM-JAY beneficiaries should be 

28 
 
given wide publicity through Community Radio, wall calendars and kiosks installed at EHCPs. 
Kerala's model of kiosks as a one-step solution should be encouraged.  
(Para 3.1.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.4.2 AB PM-JAY has a comprehensive media and outreach strategy to spread awareness and 
empower beneficiaries regarding their rights and entitlements focussing on rural areas. This 
includes intensive advertisement over traditional media platforms. NHA has shared model IEC 
materials including leaflets, flyers, pamphlets, banners etc. with the States/UTs. States/UTs 
customise these contents with respect to their regional language. NHA has been telecasting PM-
JAY related information on Doordarshan, DD News, Sansad TV, private news channels etc. 
Further, radio campaigns have been launched on AIR and private FM channels. Regular print 
advertisements are published. Other media channels like auto-branding, announcements at 
railway stations, mass-messaging, out-door branding, etc. have been undertaken. In radio, TVC 
and print-advertisement content in the local languages are used. Further, NHA has shared 
branding materials with SHA for use in local languages. Nukkad Nataks have been organised 
during events and fairs like IITF. States have organised many local events like run for Ayushman 
Bharat, painting and slogan writing competition etc. Further, many Ayushman Samvads have 
been organised with different stakeholders for reaching out to them. Also, beneficiary interaction 
sessions have also been telecasted on All India Radio (AIR) and Doordarshan.  
2.4.3 Along with this, it may kindly be noted that SHAs are extensively engaging Field Level 
Workers (FLWs) including ASHA in the Ayushman Card creation process. Also, few States have 
engaged Fair Price Shops (FPS) in Ayushman card creation.  It may be noted that in many States, 
FLWs are being incentivized by paying ₹ 5 for each successful e-KYC related to Ayushman card 
creation. 
2.4.4  It is pertinent to note that Beneficiary verification and card creation have been simplified 
with the launch of ‘Ayushman’ mobile application. This mobile application is equipped with 
face-auth technology that eliminates the dependency on any external authentication device. 
Mobile application is being leveraged for door-to-door campaign. 
2.4.5 Various campaigns like Ayushman Bhava and Viksit Bharat Sankalp Yatra (VBSY) have 
also been launched across the country to ensure saturation of Ayushman card creation.  During 
Ayushman Bhava campaign, over 9.6 crore verification requests for Ayushman card have been 
received, out of which approximately 9.42 crore Ayushman Cards have been created. Further, 2.8 
crore Ayushman cards have been created during VBSY. 
2.4.6 With respect to verification of genuine beneficiary, it is pertinent to note that the process 
of beneficiary verification has been based on Aadhaar authentication.  
 

29 
 
Recommendation 
2.4.7 The report of NITI Aayog highlighted the issue of low financial protection for health in 
the missing middle segment of the population. There are some States where the target set to cover 
the population under the PM-JAY scheme has not been met through identifying beneficiaries as 
per the SECC database and other digital databases available with the States. The Committee, in 
view of the findings of the NITI Aayog, is of the view that such States should include new 
categories for 100% targeted coverage under the scheme. This will also address the issue 
highlighted by NITI Aayog. Further, the expansion of health insurance / assurance coverage is a 
necessary step to achieve UHC. Hence, the outreach and base of beneficiaries to be covered 
under the PM-JAY scheme should be gradually increased till UHC is achieved. 
(Para 3.1.5 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.4.8 The beneficiary base under AB PM-JAY has been increasing over the years. Initially, 
when the scheme was launched, 10.74 crore beneficiary families under AB PM-JAY were 
targeted on the basis of the Socio-economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data, which was 
increased to 12 crores in 2022. Further, States/UTs were given flexibility to use other databases 
for verification of beneficiaries under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY against such SECC 
beneficiaries who couldn't be identified and verified. Accordingly, all States/UTs have provided 
beneficiary database for unidentified families and same have been ingested in beneficiary 
identification system. Further, coverage have been expanded to vulnerable groups like PVTG,

Recommendation

3.3 Empanelment of Hospitals and Management 
Recommendation 
3.3.1 The Committee recommends that NHA and SHAs should ensure that the EHCPs follow all 
the norms and safety measures. The physical verification process should be followed earnestly to 
ensure that only those hospitals are empanelled that fulfil the requisite criteria. The Ministry 
should ensure that the periodic social audits of EHCPs, involving beneficiaries, are carried out 
effectively in coordination with NHA and SHAs so that malpractices may get detected and action 
may be initiated against the errant EHCPs. Consequently, this will also ensure that benchmarks 
for discharging social responsibilities are adhered to by EHCPs. There is also a strong need to 
invest in public hospitals to improve and upgrade the quality of the existing health facilities. The 
Committee believes that these steps would help in building an effective and accountable network 
of health service providers as per quality standards.  
(Para 2.5.7 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.3.2 NHA has developed guidelines for empanelment of hospitals under AB PM-JAY wherein 
hospitals are empanelled post physical verification and subject to fulfilment of certain minimum 

39 
 
criteria. However, SHAs have been provided flexibility regarding the empanelment criteria due to 
varying situation of demand and supply, and unique geographical situations in different States. 
3.3.3 Further, all public hospitals with inpatient facilities are deemed empanelled under PM-
JAY without any physical verification. Therefore, physical verification for empanelment of 
public hospitals is not mandated.  
3.3.4 With regards to other observations of the Committee, following may be noted: 
1. NHA has issued guidelines to setup and operationalise District Implementation Unit 
(DIU). The officials engaged under DIU are entrusted with the task of undertaking 
periodical inspection of empanelled hospitals. Based on the report of DIU personnel, 
hospitals are directed to take remedial action and failing to do so, they will be 
recommended for de-empanelment. 
2. NHA is working on an improved version of HEM which envisages a system of self-
certification as well as inspection and making this information available in public domain 
in an appropriate way.  
3. Under PM-JAY, Social audits have not been mandated, however there is provision of 
various other audits viz. medical audits, BIS audits, etc. to check fraud/malpractices under 
the scheme. 
4. National Health Authority has set up a National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) with the 
primary responsibility for prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under 
PM-JAY. Further, all States/UTs have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State 
level to instrumentalize anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level. 
5. NHA has been using technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning 
(ML) technologies to detect suspicious transactions / potential frauds in AB PM-JAY. 
These technologies are being used to realize the objectives of prevention, detection and 
deterrence of healthcare frauds that could occur in AB PM-JAY. Technologies deployed 
include rule-based triggers and Machine Learning algorithms, fuzzy logic, image 
classification and de-duplication, etc. They are helpful in ensuring appropriate treatment 
is provided to the eligible beneficiaries. 
6. Suspicious claims identified by NAFU are forwarded to the various SAFUs for desk and 
field investigation. Based on the investigation report, necessary penal action is initiated 
against the errant entity. 
7. With respect to public hospitals, it is pertinent to note that public hospitals are reimbursed 
for the services provided under the scheme at par with private hospitals in addition to the 
existing budgetary support from the Government to these public hospitals. The funds 
released to public hospitals are expected to be used for the purpose of augmenting the 
amenities including upgradation of health infrastructure, engaging the medical 
professionals for providing services to the beneficiaries, etc. There are numerous 
examples of hospitals who have improved the services significantly using the funds 
reimbursed under the scheme. 

40 
 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.5 The Committee appreciates the efforts undertaken by the Ministry regarding the 
empanelment of hospitals and subsequent management through various guidelines and 
audits that has been put in place for the same. With regard, to the recommendation of the 
Committee on the requirement of social audit, the Ministry has replied that the same is not 
mandated under PM-JAY. Here, the Committee would appreciate if the Ministry could 
include social audit among other audits and utilise it as evaluation method to understand 
and amplify the service delivery of the Scheme. The relevance of a social audit is that the 
feedback would be a first-hand report from a beneficiary. Accordingly, the Committee 
would like to ingeminate its recommendation that the Ministry should ensure periodic 
social audits of EHCPs, involving beneficiaries. 
Recommendation 
3.3.6 The Committee observes that failure to provide all available specialities by EHCPs 
reduces the availability of such services to beneficiaries. The Ministry, in coordination with NHA 
and SHAs, should ensure that all the specialities available in EHCPs are empanelled under 
PMJAY. Missing specialities should be empanelled in a time-bound manner. There is also a 
strong need to upgrade the speciality services available in EHCPs in all districts across the 
country as the lack of speciality services compels the beneficiaries to move off places, which 
causes hardship and a great amount of inconvenience, besides adding to the OOPE. 
(Para 2.5.9 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.3.7 The empanelment guideline requires the hospitals to request for empanelment of all the 
specialities, however, it is not necessary that the request of the hospital for empanelment will be 
accepted for all the specialities for which it has applied due to speciality specific eligibility. 
3.3.8 It is pertinent to note that NHA has issued guideline (OM number: S-
12015/146/2021/HA(HPQA) dated 13th October 2022) wherein States are allowed to consider 
selective empanelment of eligible healthcare providers for tertiary care specialities only. This is 
expected to increase access to such specialities for PM-JAY beneficiaries. 
3.3.9 Also, NHA is deploying HEM 2.0 shortly wherein hospitals would be required to declare 
about the available specialities, at the time of empanelment request as well as at the periodic 
intervals. 
3.3.10 NHA has issued guidelines to setup and operationalise District Implementation Unit 
(DIU). The officials engaged under DIU is entrusted with the task of undertaking periodic 
inspections of empanelled hospitals. Based on the report of DIU personnel, hospitals will be 
directed to take remedial action and failing which necessary action will be taken.  

41 
 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.11 The Committee noted the Ministry's reply. The Committee is of the view that since 
PM-JAY aims for Universal Health Coverage, the NHA should review hospital 
empanelment guidelines to ensure all specialities are available to beneficiaries. This would 
increase access and reduce patients' need to travel for treatment.  The Committee also 
recommends for a system to be evolved to monitor that all the specialities available in a 
particular empanelled hospital should be made available to a beneficiary under the PM-
JAY scheme. The HEM 2.0 application should be implemented promptly to provide real-
time access to hospital specialities.  
 
Recommendation 
3.3.12 The Committee has been informed that the average available bed size is roughly 48 beds 
per EHCP. This indicates that most of the hospitals/institutions empanelled under PM-JAY are of 
small scale, and many of the bigger hospitals/institutions are not empanelled under the scheme. 
The Ministry informed that most of these hospitals are in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns and fewer in 
Tier-1 or metropolitan cities, and they are in a constant process of engagement with all bigger 
hospital chains to persuade them to join PMJAY. The Government should examine why larger 
hospitals are not joining the scheme and make efforts to empanel them. The Committee also 
recommends that the health facilities falling under the following categories be mandatorily 
empanelled: 
i. health facilities availing tax benefits. 
ii. those receiving land grants/ concessions from the Centre/ State Governments for their 
establishment. 
iii. facilities affiliated with medical colleges; and 
iv. any other category deemed fit by the Government. 
(Para 2.5.10 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.3.13 As of 14th May, 2024, a total of 29,387 hospitals including 12 464 private hospitals with 
more than 13.7 lakh beds have been empanelled under the scheme. Of these, a total of 7,161 
hospitals empanelled under AB PM-JAY are 50 or more bedded, while 3,174 hospitals are 100 or 
more bedded. 429 hospitals which are 500 or more bedded have also been empanelled under the 
scheme. Further, out of the total empanelled hospitals, 238 Medical colleges have also been 
empanelled under AB PM-JAY.  
3.3.14 Further, NHA has actively engaged with various central ministries such as the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Home Affairs to identify and 

42 
 
empanel hospitals run by these ministries. As on 14th May 2024, there are 601 Central 
Government hospitals have been empanelled under AB PM-JAY.  
3.3.15 In addition to this, all Government hospitals with in-patient services or daycare facilities 
are deemed empanelled under AB PM-JAY. Accordingly, smaller hospitals are also empanelled 
under the scheme. In addition, there are many single speciality hospitals which cater to high-end 
treatment for such specialities. The empanelment policy of the scheme aims at ensuring access to 
quality healthcare services at the closest facility. Therefore, the average bed strength under the 
scheme is reduced due to empanelment of smaller public hospitals. 
3.3.16 With regard to mandating participation of certain categories of private hospitals, it may 
kindly be noted that public health being a state subject, any such decision will have to be taken 
by respective State Government. State Health Agencies (SHAs) are mandated with the 
responsibility of empanelling hospitals under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY as per State-specific 
regulations.  
 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.17 The Committee takes note of the reply of the Ministry in this regard. The Committee 
understands that State Health Agencies (SHAs) are mandated with the responsibility of 
empanelling hospitals under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY as per State-specific regulations. 
However, the Committee still believes that since PM- JAY is a central sector scheme, the 
Central Government will be well with its rights to issue appropriate directives to the States 
to mandatorily empanel health services under PM-JAY which have availed benefits from 
the Government under the following categories:-  
i. health facilities availing tax benefits. 
ii. those receiving land grants/ concessions from the Centre/ State Governments for 
their establishment. 
iii. facilities affiliated with medical colleges; and 
iv. any other such category deemed fit by the Government. 
 
 
 
3.4 Best Practices in Providing UHC 
Recommendation 
3.4.1 The Committee observes that the daily audit system by the dedicated audit team, as 
adopted by the states of Uttarakhand and Nagaland, aided in detecting fraudulent practices, 
improved quality and time of claim processing, and effective implementation of the scheme. The 
Committee also appreciates the IT-enabled beneficiary feedback and redressal system developed 

43 
 
in Punjab. The sharing of experiences and feedback by beneficiaries after obtaining the treatment 
services helps in monitoring the quality of services and checks for illegal activities. The 
Committee is of the opinion that a robust daily audit system and the IT-enabled automated 
feedback and redressal system should be established at the district level in all the States/UTs. 
(Para 3.1.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.4.2 In the existing AB PM-JAY ecosystem, Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) have been 
integrated into the AB PM-JAY Transaction Management System (TMS) to aid the Pre-
authorising Panel Doctor (PPD) and Claims Panel Doctor (CPD) of third party administrators 
(TPAs), insurance companies and SHAs while processing a pre-authorisation request or a claim 
by specifying the mandatory documentation required and specific information to look for in these 
documents for the prescribed procedure.  Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) aims to help in 
preventing and controlling fraud and abuse. Further, the Transaction Management System (TMS) 
has established protocols for beneficiary treatment and claim adjudication. Also, there are four 
levels in claims adjudication process and States have further flexibility to add more levels based 
on their assessment and availability of resources. 
3.4.3 Also, National Health Authority has setup a National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) with the 
primary responsibility for prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under PM-
JAY. Further, all States/UTs have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State level to 
instrumentalize anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level. 
3.4.4 NHA has been using technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning 
(ML) technologies to detect suspicious transactions / potential frauds in AB PM-JAY. These 
technologies are being used to realize the objectives of prevention, detection and deterrence of 
healthcare frauds that could occur in AB PM-JAY. Technologies deployed include rule-based 
triggers and Machine Learning algorithms, fuzzy logic, image classification and de-duplication, 
etc. They are helpful in ensuring appropriate treatment is provided to the eligible beneficiaries. 
3.4.5 Suspicious claims identified by NAFU are forwarded to the various SAFUs for desk and 
field investigation. Based on the investigation report, necessary penal action is initiated against 
the errant entity. 
3.4.6 Along with this, it is important to note that NHA has a robust system of beneficiary 
empowerment and collecting feedback from the beneficiaries. Two levels of beneficiaries’ 
feedback collection are as follows: 
● Outbound feedback calls to the beneficiaries done on the second day of the discharge for 
assessing beneficiaries’ satisfaction level. 
● Health status calls done on the 15th day after discharge to check the health status of the 
beneficiary. 

44 
 
3.4.7 Along with this, a robust grievance redressal system has also been designed where 
beneficiaries can easily register and track the grievances. In case of any grievance, the 
beneficiary may register their grievances through online/offline mode. Beneficiaries can register 
grievances online through the portal https://cgrms.pmjay.gov.in or through Centralized Public 
Grievance Redressal and Monitoring System at (pgportal.gov.in). These grievances are forwarded 
to State Grievance Nodal Officer (SGNO) and further to National Grievance Nodal Officer 
(NGNO) for necessary action. The complainant can track the status of their grievances through 
the portal itself. For offline grievances, beneficiaries can call on the helpline ‘14588’ where 
complaint is registered through call centre executives.  
Further Recommendation 
3.4.8 The Committee has noted the reply of the Ministry. But, the Committee would like 
the Ministry to explore the merit in daily audit system akin to the states of Uttarakhand 
and Nagaland, which has proven to be quite effective.  
 
3.5 Quality of Healthcare Services and health infrastructure 
Recommendation 
3.5.1 Maintaining the quality of healthcare services across a vast network of public and private 
providers is challenging. Variability in the quality of care can affect patient outcomes. The 
Committee has observed that most of the Government hospitals are not up to the standard in 
cleanliness, infrastructure, and the treatment of the patients. These hospitals are not patient 
friendly. The Government must take steps to make Government hospitals patient-friendly, ensure 
quality cleanliness and upgrade the basic infrastructure. The Ministry, through the Health 
Secretaries across the States, should have a periodic report on cleanliness and infrastructure in 
those hospitals. Government hospitals may be rated like private hospitals under NABH. 
(Para 3.2.3(i) (a) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.5.2 Under AB PM-JAY, all Government hospitals with in-patient services are deemed 
empanelled. 
3.5.3 Further, public hospitals are reimbursed for the services provided under the scheme at par 
with private hospitals. The funds released to public hospitals are expected to be used for the 
purpose of upgrading the health infrastructure and providing better amenities to the beneficiaries. 
Also, the hospitals certified with NQAS are given additional incentive of 15% as incentive. Thus, 
hospitals are recognised and rewarded for providing quality care. 
3.5.4 Public health is a state subject, therefore, the overall responsibility regarding the 
upgradation of facilities in public health institutions lies with the respective State Government. 

45 
 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.5.5 The Committee emphasizes that the overarching objective of the Central 
Government along with all the State Governments and Union Territories (UTs) is to provide 
high-quality and state-of-the-art healthcare facilities aiming at attaining UHC. 
Consequently, the significance of establishing advanced medical infrastructure throughout 
the country cannot be overlooked. Considering this, the Committee is of the view that a 
collaborative approach may be adopted, urging all State Governments and UTs to work in 
tandem with the Central Government to address this critical issue. The current scenario 
concerning health infrastructure calls for the implementation of a structured mechanism, 
including clearly defined guidelines applicable to all government hospitals nationwide. Such 
an initiative would not only enhance the quality of healthcare services but also ensure that 
the medical facilities are equipped to meet contemporary health challenges effectively.  
 
Recommendation  
3.5.6 The Committee is of the view that the cost of medicines, particularly in cases of diseases 
like cancer where long-term treatment is required, is also a matter of concern. The Government 
should consider providing medicines free of cost to all the beneficiaries across the States through 
the PMJAY scheme. 
(Para 3.2.3(v) (d) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.5.7 AB PM-JAY covers treatment during IPD services including pre-hospitalization expenses 
up to 3 days, and post-hospitalization expenses including drug expenses for up to 15-days. Also, 
certain drugs are provided by Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs).  
Further Recommendation 
3.5.8 The Committee while taking into cognizance the reply of the Ministry, would like to 
reiterate its view on covering the cost of medicines, particularly in cases of diseases like 
cancer where long-term treatment is required, under AB PM-JAY. The Committee 
acknowledges that it would be a special provision. Since the Ministry itself had made a 
submission before the Committee that within the limit of ₹ 5 lakhs, 99.4% of expenditure 
incurred per treatment cycle is usually below ₹ 2 lakhs and the existing wallet of ₹ 5 lakhs is 
sufficient for providing treatment to the beneficiaries. The Committee wants the Ministry 
to explore the window provided by this difference to incorporate the component of covering 
the cost of medicines, particularly in cases of diseases like cancer, etc.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  - AT   A  GLANCE 
 
Healthcare Access and Affordability in India 
The Committee acknowledges the advancements made in health sector expenditure by the 
Government. However, it would like to underscore the need for a critical examination of 
these developments considering the National Health Policy (NHP) 2017. The Government 
has set an ambitious target to elevate public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP. As per 
recent PIB Press release there has been an increase in health expenditure from 1.4% to 
1.9% between the fiscal years 2017-18 and 2023-24. While this upward trend is noticeable, it 
is essential to recognize that the target set by the Government remains a significant 
challenge to achieve. The Committee emphasizes that substantial efforts are still required to 
meet this target. Therefore, it recommends that the Government realign its strategies and 
preparedness to intensify efforts towards achieving the stipulated goal. Additionally, the 
Committee urges upon the Government to submit a comparative analysis of the progress 
made by various States and Union Territories (UTs) concerning the NHP 2017 mandate, 
which stipulates that States should allocate at least 8% of their budgets to health spending. 
This data will facilitate a comprehensive understanding and evaluation of progress in health 
expenditure across the country. Furthermore, the Committee would like to be informed 
about any obstacles impeding the realization of these targets. Identifying these hindrances 
will be crucial for devising effective strategies to enhance public health funding and ensure 
that the objectives set forth in the National Health Policy are met efficiently. 
 
(Para 3.1.11 of the ATR) 
 
Coverage of beneficiaries under PMJAY 
 
The Committee takes note of explanation given by the Ministry.  But, the Ministry has not 
addressed the recommendation of the Committee regarding the difficulties being faced by 
the beneficiaries having family size less than or more than 6 members. Accordingly, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation and would like the Ministry to furnish a reply on 
the issue. 
(Para 3.2.6 of the ATR) 
 
The Committee finds that the reply of the Government only mentions efforts undertaken by 
the Government to spread awareness about PMJAY. While the recommendation of the 
Committee was related to identification and registration of eligible beneficiaries is the last 
mile challenge in actual enrolment. For this, measures like intensive registration campaigns 
under the auspices of Local Self Government Institutions, ASHAs, AWWs workers, etc 
should be considered. Such campaigns should include door to door registration, 
organisation of registration camps, etc wherein problems related to low literacy, limited

gains immense importance in the wake of introduction of health insurance cover of up to

get them registered as beneficiaries. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that 
immediate measure be undertaken by the Government in this direction to make this 
coveted Scheme an effective one.

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and 
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this 160th Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the Government on the 
Recommendations/ Observations contained in the 155th Report on Functioning of Central 
Government Health Scheme (CGHS).

Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table 
of the Lok Sabha on8th February 2024. The Action Taken Notes of the Government on the 
recommendations contained in the Report were received from the Departments in the Month of 
July, 2024.

recommendations/ observations, in respect of which replies of the Government, have not been 
accepted by the Committee and the Committee has made further recommendations thereon and has 
been categorized under Chapter-III. While 02 recommendations/observations in respect of which 
final replies of the Government have not been received, have been categorized under Chapter-IV. 
4. The Committee, in its meeting held on the 18th December, 2024 considered the Draft Report 
and adopted the same.

THE GOVERNMENT 
 
1.1 BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR CGHS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.1.1 The Committee recommends the Ministry implement measures aimed at maximizing 
the utilisation of funds allocated to the CGHS. Furthermore, the Ministry should establish a 
robust mechanism to ensure optimal utilisation of these funds and curb any instances of 
wasteful expenditure. This proactive approach will ensure the judicious use of resources and 
enhance the overall efficiency of the CGHS. 
(Para 1.4.3 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 To ensure maximum and effective utilization of allocated budget to CGHS, the 
following mechanism has been adopted: 
 
(i) the senior officers of the Ministry and CGHS are monitoring the progress of works 
by holding regularly meeting with Additional Director of CGHS cities, 
 
(ii) Standard Operating Procedure guidelines have also been framed for timely 
execution of construction work in particular Financial Year, which provides that 
proposals may be planned in preceding financial year and should be submitted in 1st 
week of April so that timely approvals can be conveyed and work completed in that 
Financial Year, 
 
(iii) Monthly Expenditure Plan and Quarterly Expenditure Plan are prepared and 
accordingly expenditures are incurred.  
 
1.2 INFRASTRUCTURE IN A CGHS WC 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.2.1 The Committee has learned about the poor infrastructure of some wellness centres,

1.3 STAFFING UNDER CGHS 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.3.1 The Committee noted an additional requirement of about 20 to 30 % of the sanctioned 
strength of doctors, paramedical and administrative staff, over and above the sanctioned 
strength, in all CGHS set-ups across the country. The additional requirement for a Junior 
Health Administrative Assistant is around 70% of the present sanctioned strength. Further, 
during the deliberation, the Ministry informed the Committee that a considerable percentage 
of the sanctioned strength of medical and administrative staff is also lying vacant. This leads 
to a poor doctor-to-beneficiary ratio, long waiting times for patients in CGHS dispensaries, 
and a decrease in the quality of patient care. 
(Para 2.4.3 of the Report) 
 
 
1.3.2 The Committee is of the view that opening or operating CGHS centres without 
sufficient doctors and staff has no meaning and causes inconvenience to beneficiaries. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry expedite the recruitment process and fill 
up all vacant positions. To ensure an adequate doctor-to-patient ratio in all CGHS wellness 
centres, the recommendations of SIU may be implemented expeditiously. Based on the total 
number of beneficiaries being served by a Wellness centre, minimum criteria for doctors to 
see the patients per day may be fixed and strictly adhered to. On being enquired, the Ministry 
informed that around 500 contractual doctors have been engaged in addition to regular 
doctors to improve the doctor-to-beneficiary ratio. 
(Para 2.4.4 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.3 Requisition of 584 vacancies for GDMOs for all over India posting has already been 
placed before UPSC to be filled through CMSE - 2023. Recruitment against vacant posts is a 
continuous process. For Group B (Non Gazetted) and Group C direct recruitment posts under 
CGHS, recruitment is being done through Staff Selection Commission (SSC) by the 
designated Zonal Heads/ADs (i.e. CGHS Delhi, CGHS Prayagraj, CGHS Kolkata, CGHS 

3 
 
Mumbai, CGHS Chennai, CGHS Chandigarh, CGHS Bengaluru, CGHS Guwahati and CGHS 
Bhopal).

Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) meetings for the promotional posts under their 
respective administrative control. During the Mission Recruitment of Government of India 
(monitored by DoPT), around 1200 vacant Group B (NG) and Group C posts (including posts 
of Junior Health Administrative Assistants) have been reported to SSC. 
 
1.4 AVAILABILITY AND QUALITY OF MEDICINES SUPPLIED AT 
WELLNESS CENTRES 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.4.1 The Committee is further of the view that the course of some of the medicines, like 
antibiotics, is required to be started by the patients on the same day or immediately, as 
prescribed by the medical officer of the dispensary or by the doctor of the empanelled HCOs 
(visited after a referral from the dispensary). In case such medicine is not readily available in 
the dispensary, the same is indented. A patient cannot wait for two days to receive that 
indented medicine, and the procedure of buying directly from the ALC and getting the same 
reimbursed later causes inconvenience to the patient, who should rest to recover early instead 
of running from pillar to post. The Committee, therefore, feels that the turnaround time to 
receive indented medicine should be reduced to less than 24 hours. The Ministry should make 
necessary course corrections to ensure that the indented medicines are available by the very 
next day morning. 
 (Para 2.5.3 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.4.2 This practice is already incorporated in the terms and conditions of ALC supply. Due 
care is taken to supply medicine the next day, such as antibiotics and other emergency 
medicines.

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.5.1 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry to ensure timely settlement of 
bills despite functioning under different kinds of constraints. However, the Committee 
observed that many bills due for payment are carried over to the next financial year owing to 
various reasons, which is affecting the credibility of CGHS. It is one of the major reasons for 
refusal of treatment to CGHS beneficiaries by some of the empanelled hospitals. The 
Committee simultaneously observes that the empanelled hospitals are in financial distress 
because of outstanding dues from CGHS. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry establishes a mechanism for daily review of pending bills to ensure that the

processing of bills gets smoother and disbursements are made seamlessly. The Ministry 
should fix a turnaround time for the settlement of bills. 
 (Para 2.6.3 of the report)

1.8 REFERRAL SYSTEM UNDER CGHS 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.8.1 The Committee has, however, learnt that as per present practice, even after obtaining a 
referral in the first instance, if the consultant in the private hospital prescribes any 
tests/investigation/treatment, the beneficiary is required to report back to the dispensary and 
get that prescribed tests/investigation/treatment endorsed from the CGHS doctor. The 
Committee feels that the present referral system is cumbersome, which only inconveniences 
the beneficiaries and adds to the woes of a patient with poor health. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry devise appropriate solutions to simplify the referral system so that a 
beneficiary is not required to visit the CGHS dispensary multiple times just to get the 
prescribed tests done following a referral in the first instance. 
 
 (Para 2.11.2 of the Report) 
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.8.2 Ministry has issued revised guidelines for referral process under CGHS vide OM 
dated 28.06.2024. Now, no further endorsement from CGHS is required for undergoing 
routine listed investigations & minor procedures not requiring admission in the hospital as 
advised by the specialist within the validity period of 3 months from the date of issue of the 
initial referral. Referral/ endorsement from CGHS shall be required for special investigations 
like CT Scan, MRI Scan, PET Scan and any other investigation costing over Rs. 3,000/- and 
the referral will be valid for 3 months. In addition, the beneficiaries of age 70 years and above

with regard to monitoring and effectively delivering public services. The LAC and ZAC are 
effective platforms for interaction between the CGHS officials and local Members of 
Parliament (MPs) of the area. The Committee feels that such platforms help strengthen the 
services delivered by CGHS, as Members of Parliament, apart from being public 
representatives, are also beneficiaries themselves. Hence, their feedback in such interactions

never received a call from anybody regarding the schedule of such Committee meetings. The

also monitor the compliance of such directions by the CGHS authorities. 
 
 (Para 2.13.1 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.9.2 Ministry understands the noble cause of the matter. The Additional Director, CGHS

and submit compliance to the Directorate so that Local MPs can interact with public and 
review the functioning of CGHS facilities.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
3.1 NEED FOR AUGMENTING WELLNESS CENTRES 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.1.1 The Ministry informed that as of August 2023, the CGHS had a presence in 80 cities 
with 340 CGHS Allopathic wellness centres. The Committee has noted that out of these 340 
allopathic wellness centres, 26% are concentrated in the Delhi NCR region. Further, only six 
states (excluding the Delhi NCR region) have more than 10 CGHS centres. This highlights 
that the distribution and accessibility of CGHS services across different regions of the country 
are not equitable and need to be addressed. The Committee noted that the state of Arunachal 
Pradesh and the UTs of Ladakh, A & N islands and Lakshadweep have no CGHS wellness 
centre. 
(Para 2.2.1 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 The main reasons behind concentration of CGHS WCs in Delhi is that all Ministries/ 
Departments are situated in Delhi and majority of Head Quarters of Attached and Subordinate 
Offices of Govt. of India are situated in Delhi. However, as per the requests of beneficiaries 
and by various feasibility analysis through regular meetings, New Wellness Centres at 
different locations across the country have been opened. One such CGHS WC is already 
sanctioned for Itanagar, Arunachal Pradesh and likely to be functional soon.  
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.1.3 The Committee notes from the replies (paras 2.1.2 & 3.1.2) of the Government, 
the process of securing and release of funds for expansion of CGHS as well as the reason 
for higher concentration of CGHS Wellness Centres in Delhi NCR. However, the replies 
do not address the recommendation of the Committee about the need to further expand 
the coverage of CGHS in existing and new cities so as to have distribution and 
accessibility of CGHS services across different regions of the country in the ideal 
proportion. Accordingly, the Committee wants the Government to furnish a 
comprehensive action taken reply in this regard.   
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.1.4 The Committee is aware that there are many cities and towns where there are a 
sizeable number of Central Government employees, pensioners, and their dependents, but no 
CGHS wellness centre exists there. As a result, the beneficiaries, particularly the retired 
beneficiaries, are required to travel long distances to get medical treatments, causing 

15 
 
inconvenience to them. The Committee opines that this scenario, apart from being financially 
draining on the beneficiaries, also causes various other hardships to the beneficiaries. 
(Para 2.2.2 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
3.1.5 Opening of a new Wellness Centres are considered as per extant norms, which include 
minimum 6000 Central Government serving employees in the particular city, subject to 
availability of resources, sanction for creation of posts of Medical Officers, Staff Nurse, 
Pharmacists, and Clerical Staff etc. by the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, 
and availability of suitable accommodation for new Wellness Centre. Due to the crunch of 
resources, the Ministry takes a considerate view regarding creation of posts at an appropriate 
time. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.1.6 The Committee understands that the Ministry considers several factors when 
opening new wellness centres, including resources, creation of posts, accommodation, 
etc. The Committee has, however, noted an imbalance in the distribution of these 
centres, with 26% in Delhi NCR but only six states having more than 10 centres each. To 
address this, the Committee recommends modifying the norms, such as adjusting the 
beneficiary requirement based on area remoteness, on the lines of organisations like 
ESIC. The Committee also urge the Ministry to overcome barriers like resource 
availability and to work with the Ministry of Finance for creating necessary posts. 
 
3.2 INFRASTRUCTURE IN A CGHS WC 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.2.1 There is a lack of Ambulance service at many of the Wellness Centres. This is 
required in critical cases of referrals and emergencies. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry also consider allocating separate funds for arranging at least one ambulance in each 
Wellness Centre so that the patient can be taken to the higher medical centre promptly for 
emergency treatment. The Ministry should also prepare a model list of essential services and 
equipment that all CGHS Wellness Centres should have available. 
 (Para 2.3.2 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.2.2 CGHS WCs are providing primary health care services to the beneficiaries. For any 
emergency situation a beneficiaries have a choice to go to any nearby empanelled or Govt. 
Hospital instead of waiting at CGHS WC for ambulance. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 

16 
 
3.2.3 The Committee agrees with the contention of the Ministry that CGHS wellness 
centres are providing primary health care services to the beneficiaries and in any 
emergency situation, the beneficiary has the option to visit nearby empanelled or 
Government hospital. But the Ministry has not responded to the recommendation of the 
Committee regarding the model list of essential services and equipments. Hence, the 
Committee is reiterating its recommendation on the importance for having a model list 
of essential services and equipments that should be available in the Wellness centre and 
post that list on its website and the reception area of the respective Wellness centre for 
information.  
 
3.3 AVAILABILITY AND QUALITY OF MEDICINES SUPPLIED AT 
WELLNESS CENTRES 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.1 It has come to the Committee’s notice that the medicines are often not procured 
promptly, causing inconvenience to the beneficiaries. In many cases, the bid/ contract of the 
ALC are not renewed well in time, and the dispensary is not in a position to supply the 
medicines. 
(Para 2.5.1 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.2 Utmost care is taken to supply the medicines promptly to the beneficiaries from the 
Wellness centres (MSD and Jan Aushadhi Supply or through ALC). ALC contracts are being 
renewed well on time so that no inconvenience occurs to the patients.  
 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.3 The Committee recommends the Ministry to investigate the issues of delay in 
procurement and subsequent distribution of medicines. The Ministry may bring necessary 
changes in the guidelines and simplify the procedure for the local purchase of medicines to 
ensure an uninterrupted supply of medicines. The Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry establish a mechanism to ensure the continuous availability of basic/ essential 
medicines at CGHS dispensaries so that the need for local purchase does not arise. The 
Ministry should take necessary steps towards course correction, including making the 
required funds available for regular supply of medicines.  
(Para 2.5.2 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.4 Application Program Interface (API) has been developed and is in place, with which 
the MSO and MSD can observe their stock position and supplies in pipeline. Drug Vaccine 
Distribution and Management System (DVDMS) is in place in MSO, which has improved our 
inventory management and distribution.   
 
Recommendations/Observations  

17 
 
3.3.5 The Committee has come to know that there are complaints regarding the quality of 
medicines disbursed at the pharmacy counter of the dispensary. Questions have been raised 
regarding the effectiveness of medicines procured through MSO and JAP. The quality of 
medicines is of paramount importance while providing healthcare services, and complaints 
regarding the quality should be taken seriously. This is also essential to ensure compliance 
with the Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards of the World Health Organization 
(WHO). The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry establish a mechanism ensuring 
rigorous testing of medicines. The Ministry may inspect these laboratories and surprise test 
any random batch of medicines through any third independent NABL-accredited laboratory. 
The Ministry may also consider testing random batches of medicines from a reputed 
international laboratory. 
 (Para 2.5.5 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.6 A quality assurance and inspection protocol is already in place by MSO, for the supply 
of medicines to its CGHS. Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) has a 
quality assurance protocol in place, where testing is already being done by an NABL certified 
laboratory. Random testing, as per the Committee’s observation is already being done. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.3.7 In replies (paras 3.3.2, 3.3.4 & 3.3.6) to recommendations of the Committee 
related to delay in procurement & subsequent distribution of medicines, supply of 
medicines and quality of medicines disbursed at the pharmacy counter of the 
dispensary, the Ministry gave an account of the extant systems in place for addressing 
the issues. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that if the existing 
systems were foolproof, there would not have been so many complaints/grievances upon 
which the Committee felt the need to recommend. Therefore, the Committee reiterates 
its recommendations and wants the Ministry to review the existing systems and suggest 
some effective measures to mitigate these persisting problems.

Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.4.1 The Ministry may consider periodic meetings of CGHS authorities with the HCOs at 
the regional level to deliberate upon the regularly raised objections, which HCOs can correct 
in future. The Government may also consider payment to HCOs using predictive statistical 
analysis/tools about the cost of treatment. This can enable the system to determine the rentage 
of the amount to be deducted and thereafter, release the balance amount automatically. Such a 
step will be in the interest of both the beneficiaries and HCOs and will also, to some extent, 
address the grievances related to denial of treatment by hospitals. 
 (Para 2.6.4 of the report) 
Action Taken 

18 
 
 
3.4.2 It will be in the interest of all stakeholders to have periodic meetings with the HCOs 
and the same may be arranged including all the stake holders like CPDS, SAs and DDOs etc 
for smooth and efficient functioning of the system. Regarding payment to HCOs using 
predictive statistical analysis/tools about the cost of treatment, it is a policy decision. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.4.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry agrees with the observation that periodic 
meeting with HCOs is in the interest of all stakeholders. Further, the Committee would 
like to be apprised about the mechanism established by the Ministry to ensure periodic 
deliberative meetings between the CGHS authorities and HCOs to discuss the regularly 
raised objections. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that payment to 
HCOs using predictive statistical analysis/tools about the cost of treatment is a policy 
decision. The Committee would like the Government to consider this recommendation at 
the policy level. This is in interest of both the beneficiaries and HCOs, and would 
address their grievances in an effective manner.
